notes.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes
notes.answer: It shows that the reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.
notes.explanation: Some reactions proceed only forwards, while others can proceed both forwards and backwards under the same conditions. In a reversible reaction, products can react to form the original reactants.
notes.simple: Some changes can go both ways. Other changes go only forwards.
examples: NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) is an irreversible reaction that goes to completion.
CuSO₄ · 5 H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5 H₂O(g) shows the reversible change between hydrated and anhydrous copper sulphate.
steps: Identify whether the reaction can proceed in both directions under the same conditions.
If it proceeds only forwards, call it irreversible and use →.
If products can form reactants again, call it reversible and use ⇌.
Check whether a product escapes or is removed, because this can make a reversible reaction go to completion.
notes.checkAnswer: A reversible reaction proceeds in both directions under the same conditions; an irreversible reaction proceeds only in the forward direction.

notes.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
notes.answer: The reaction continues in both directions at equal rates, so the concentrations of reacting species remain constant.
notes.explanation: In dynamic equilibrium, a reversible reaction continues in both directions. The forward and backward reactions happen at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
notes.simple: The reaction has not stopped. Both directions keep happening, but they balance each other, so the amounts of reactants and products do not change.
examples: In a sealed flask, colourless N₂O₄ changes into brown NO₂. As NO₂ forms, the reverse reaction also starts; at equilibrium, the brown colour stops changing.
In a closed container of water at a fixed temperature, evaporation and condensation can occur at equal rates.
steps: A reversible reaction starts in the forward direction.
Products build up and begin to react in the backward direction.
The forward and backward reaction rates become equal.
The reaction continues in both directions, while concentrations stay constant.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the concentrations of reactants and products at dynamic equilibrium?
notes.checkAnswer: At dynamic equilibrium, forward and backward reaction rates are equal, and the concentrations remain constant.

notes.title: Changing conditions at equilibrium
notes.answer: A catalyst increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions, so equilibrium is reached in less time.
notes.explanation: A reversible reaction at equilibrium can be disturbed by changing the amounts of reactants or products, the temperature, or—when gases are involved—the pressure. The reaction then shifts in a direction that helps establish equilibrium again. A catalyst makes equilibrium happen sooner but does not change the equilibrium position.
notes.simple: If you disturb an equilibrium, the reaction shifts to help restore it. A catalyst only helps it get there faster.
examples: Adding N₂ to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) makes the reaction move forward and form more NH₃.
Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), that is the forward side.
steps: Identify what changed: the amount of a substance, temperature, or pressure.
For a changed amount, note whether a reactant or product was added or removed.
For temperature, use whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
For pressure, compare the total moles of gaseous substances on both sides.
Remember that a catalyst speeds up both directions and reduces the time to reach equilibrium.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a catalyst do to a reversible reaction at equilibrium?
notes.checkAnswer: The forward and backward reaction rates increase equally; the catalyst makes equilibrium take less time to reach.

notes.title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium
notes.answer: No. Both reactions continue, but at equal rates.
notes.explanation: At equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates. The amounts of reactants and products stay constant, but the reactions have not stopped.
notes.simple: Think of two equally fast streams of people moving in opposite directions. People are still moving, but the number on each side stays the same.
examples: For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), both sides have two moles of gas, so increasing pressure does not favour either direction.
For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), high pressure favours ammonia because the product side has fewer gas molecules.
steps: A reversible reaction can go in both the forward and backward directions.
In a closed system, the forward reaction starts and products begin to form.
As products build up, the backward reaction rate increases.
At equilibrium, forward and backward reaction rates are equal.
A change in temperature, pressure, or concentration can shift the equilibrium position.
notes.checkQuestion: At dynamic equilibrium, have the forward and backward reactions stopped?
notes.checkAnswer: The concentrations of reactants and products stay constant because the forward and backward reaction rates are equal.

The white anhydrous salt loses all its colour permanently.
The salt changes into calcium carbonate.
rationales: This is correct because it becomes hydrated copper sulphate, which is blue.
The textbook describes a blue solid forming, not a green gas.
The change is reversible: absorbing moisture makes the salt blue again.
Calcium carbonate is a different compound and is not the product of this change.

quiz.stem: What colour is hydrated cobalt chloride hexahydrate according to this section?
options: Blue
Pink
Purple
White
rationales: Blue is the colour of anhydrous cobalt chloride in the section.
This is correct because hydrated cobalt chloride hexahydrate is pink.
Purple is the colour of cobalt chloride dihydrate, not the hexahydrate.
White is the colour change described for heated copper sulphate, not hydrated cobalt chloride.

quiz.stem: When anhydrous cobalt chloride absorbs limited moisture and then more moisture, what colours are formed in order?
options: The dihydrate is purple and the hexahydrate is pink.
The dihydrate is pink and the hexahydrate is purple.
Both the dihydrate and hexahydrate are blue.
Both the dihydrate and hexahydrate are white.
rationales: This is correct: limited moisture forms the purple dihydrate, and further moisture forms the pink hexahydrate.
This reverses the colours given for the two hydrated forms in the textbook.
Blue is the colour of anhydrous cobalt chloride, not both hydrated forms.
The textbook gives purple and pink for these hydrated forms, not white.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium?
options: Both reactions stop completely.
The forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
All reactants have changed into products.
The backward reaction becomes faster than the forward reaction.
rationales: This is wrong because the reaction continues rather than stopping.
This is right because equal rates keep the concentrations constant while both reactions continue.
This is wrong because equilibrium does not require all reactants to be used up.
This is wrong because at equilibrium the backward rate is equal to, not greater than, the forward rate.

quiz.stem: What happens to the concentrations of reacting species when dynamic equilibrium has been reached?
options: They keep increasing.
They keep decreasing.
They remain constant.
They become zero.
rationales: This is wrong because the forward reaction is balanced by the backward reaction.
This is wrong because the backward reaction is balanced by the forward reaction.
This is right because equal reaction rates mean there is no overall change in concentration.
This is wrong because equilibrium does not mean that all reacting species disappear.

quiz.stem: Why is chemical equilibrium called dynamic?
options: Only the forward reaction continues.
Only the backward reaction continues.
Both reactions continue.
Neither reaction can occur.
rationales: This is wrong because the backward reaction also continues at equilibrium.
This is wrong because the forward reaction also continues at equilibrium.
This is right because both directions keep occurring even though concentrations stay constant.
This is wrong because the reaction has not stopped.

quiz.stem: In a reversible reaction started by mixing reactants, what happens after some product has built up?
options: The forward reaction begins to slow down.
The backward reaction begins after products have built up.
The reaction becomes irreversible.
The products disappear immediately.
rationales: This is not the key event described; the important change is that the backward reaction begins.
This is right because accumulated products react to form reactants in the reverse reaction.
This is wrong because the reaction remains reversible.
This is wrong because products react backward but do not disappear immediately.

quiz.stem: What affects the time taken for a reaction to reach dynamic equilibrium?
options: It depends on the nature of the reaction and the conditions.
It is always reached instantly.
It always takes several years.
It depends only on the amount of product present.
rationales: This is right because both the reaction's nature and the conditions affect the time.
This is wrong because equilibrium is not reached instantly in every reaction.
This is wrong because some reactions reach equilibrium within seconds or minutes.
This is wrong because the time does not depend only on the amount of product.

quiz.stem: A sealed flask contains colourless N₂O₄, which forms brown NO₂. What should happen to the mixture's colour as it approaches equilibrium?
options: The colour changes from brown to colourless and then stays colourless.
The colour becomes brown and then stays at a steady shade.
The flask remains colourless because NO₂ is colourless.
The colour changes continually even after equilibrium is reached.
rationales: This is wrong because brown NO₂ forms from colourless N₂O₄.
This is right because brown NO₂ forms and the colour stops changing when concentrations become constant.
This is wrong because the section identifies NO₂ as brown.
This is wrong because the colour becomes steady when the mixture reaches equilibrium.

quiz.stem: Which statement about reaction rates at dynamic equilibrium is correct?
options: At equilibrium, the forward reaction has stopped.
At equilibrium, the backward reaction has stopped.
At equilibrium, both reactions continue at equal rates.
At equilibrium, the reactants and products have equal concentrations.
rationales: This is wrong because the forward reaction continues.
This is wrong because the backward reaction continues.
This is right because equal forward and backward rates define the dynamic state.
This is wrong because the concentrations need not be equal; they remain constant.

quiz.stem: Which observation is consistent with dynamic equilibrium?
options: A reaction can be at equilibrium only in an open container.
A reaction can be at equilibrium while its forward and backward reactions continue.
A reaction is at equilibrium when its products have all decomposed.
A reaction is at equilibrium only when there are no reactants left.
rationales: This is wrong because the section's sealed-flask example can approach equilibrium.
This is right because the reaction continues in both directions at equilibrium.
This is wrong because equilibrium does not mean all products decompose.
This is wrong because reactants remain present at equilibrium.

quiz.stem: At equilibrium, more N₂ is added to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). What happens as the system restores equilibrium?
options: More NH₃ will form.
The reaction will shift backward and form more N₂ and H₂.
The equilibrium position will not change.
The reaction will stop.
rationales: Adding a reactant makes the reaction use it by moving forward and forming more ammonia.
The backward shift would produce more of the N₂ that was already added, rather than use it.
Adding a reacting species disturbs the equilibrium and changes the concentrations.
A reversible reaction continues in both directions at equilibrium; it does not stop.

quiz.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), which direction is favoured when pressure is increased?
options: The forward reaction is favoured.
The backward reaction is favoured.
There is no effect because there are gases on both sides.
The reaction stops at once.
rationales: There are fewer moles of gas on the product side, so increased pressure favours the forward direction.
The backward direction has more gaseous moles, so it is not favoured by increased pressure.
Pressure can affect a gaseous equilibrium when the numbers of gaseous moles differ across the reaction.
Changing pressure disturbs the equilibrium; it does not make the reaction stop.

quiz.stem: The forward formation of ammonia is exothermic. What direction is favoured when the temperature is increased?
options: The forward direction.
The backward direction.
Neither direction, because temperature never affects equilibrium.
Both directions stop.
rationales: Increasing temperature does not favour the exothermic forward direction in this reaction.
The reverse direction is endothermic, so increasing temperature favours the backward direction.
Temperature can disturb equilibrium, and this section describes its effect on ammonia formation.
A temperature change shifts the equilibrium; it does not stop both reactions.

quiz.stem: What is the effect of adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction?
options: It increases only the forward reaction rate.
It increases only the backward reaction rate.
It increases both reaction rates and reduces the time taken to reach equilibrium.
It changes the equilibrium concentrations but not the reaction rates.
rationales: A catalyst increases the rates of both directions, not only the forward reaction.
A catalyst increases the rates of both directions, not only the backward reaction.
A catalyst speeds up both reactions, so the system reaches equilibrium sooner.
A catalyst affects reaction rates; it does not change the equilibrium concentrations.

quiz.stem: When can a pressure change disturb a gaseous equilibrium, and which side does increased pressure favour?
options: Equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas.
Equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas.
Pressure always favours the reactants.
Pressure has the same effect even when the gas-mole numbers are equal.
rationales: When gaseous mole numbers differ, increased pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles.
Increased pressure favours the side with fewer, not more, gaseous moles.
Pressure does not always favour reactants; the direction depends on gaseous mole numbers on both sides.
If the gaseous mole numbers are equal on both sides, a pressure change does not shift the equilibrium position.

quiz.stem: Which change can help force a reversible reaction towards completion?
options: Remove some reactant.
Add more of the product.
Remove product as it forms.
Add a catalyst and expect a larger equilibrium yield.
rationales: Removing reactant does not drive the reaction towards making more product.
Adding product does not help drive the reaction forward.
Removing product as it forms disturbs equilibrium and can drive the reaction towards further product formation.
A catalyst helps equilibrium be reached sooner but does not increase the equilibrium yield.

quiz.stem: What happens to the concentrations when an equilibrium system is left undisturbed?
options: The concentration of every species stays constant.
All forward and backward reactions stop.
The reactants are completely used up.
Only the product concentration keeps increasing.
rationales: At equilibrium, the concentrations of all participating species remain constant.
Equilibrium is dynamic: forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
A reversible reaction does not necessarily use up all its reactants at equilibrium.
At equilibrium, product concentrations do not keep increasing; they remain constant.

quiz.stem: Q6.1. What will happen if the rates of forward and reverse reactions are very high?
options: The equilibrium point will reach very soon.
The equilibrium point will reach very late.
The reaction will not attain the state of dynamic equilibrium.
The reaction will be practically irreversible.
rationales: Correct: high forward and reverse rates allow equal rates to be reached quickly.
Incorrect: high reaction rates do not make equilibrium take longer to reach.
Incorrect: reversible reactions can attain dynamic equilibrium even when both rates are high.
Incorrect: high rates do not make a reversible reaction practically irreversible.

quiz.stem: Q6.2. Predict which components of the atmosphere react in the presence of lightning.
options: N₂ and H₂O
O₂ and H₂O
CO₂ and O₂
N₂ and O₂
rationales: Incorrect: nitrogen and water are not the atmospheric components identified for this reaction.
Incorrect: oxygen and water are not the pair that reacts due to lightning in this example.
Incorrect: carbon dioxide and oxygen are not the pair that reacts due to lightning.
Correct: lightning provides energy for atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen to react.

quiz.stem: Q6.3. An inorganic chemist places one mole of PCl₃ in a container A and one mole of each Cl₂ and PCl₃ in container B. Both the containers were sealed and heated to the same temperature to reach the state of equilibrium. Guess about the composition of mixtures in both the containers.
options: Both the containers will have the same composition of mixtures.
Container A will have more concentration of PCl₃ than B.
Container A will have less concentration of PCl₃ than B.
Both the containers will have zero concentration of its reactants.
rationales: Incorrect: the different starting mixtures do not produce identical equilibrium mixtures in these containers.
Correct: container B starts with Cl₂ as well as PCl₃, so more PCl₃ is used to form product than in A.
Incorrect: this reverses the expected comparison of the PCl₃ concentrations.
Incorrect: equilibrium does not normally use up all reactants.

quiz.stem: Q6.4. CaO or lime is used extensively in steel, glass and paper industries. It is produced in an exothermic reversible reaction by the decomposition of lime (CaCO₃). Choose the conditions to produce maximum amount of lime.
options: Heating at high temperature in a closed vessel
Heating at high temperature in an open vessel
Cooling it in a closed vessel
Cooling it in an open vessel
rationales: Incorrect: a closed vessel allows CO₂ to build up, opposing further decomposition.
Correct: high temperature promotes decomposition, and an open vessel lets CO₂ escape.
Incorrect: cooling does not promote the decomposition needed to produce lime.
Incorrect: although CO₂ can escape, cooling does not favour decomposition.

quiz.stem: Q6.5. What condition should be met for the reversible reaction to achieve the state of equilibrium?
options: All the reactants should be converted into the products.
50% of the reactants should be converted into products.
The concentrations of all the reactants and the products should become constant.
One of the products should be removed from the reaction mixture.
rationales: Incorrect: at equilibrium, some reactants usually remain.
Incorrect: equilibrium does not require exactly half of the reactants to be converted.
Correct: constant concentrations are a feature of equilibrium when the forward and backward rates are equal.
Incorrect: removing a product can shift equilibrium, but it is not a condition required to attain equilibrium.

quiz.stem: Q6.6. Why the gas starts coming out when you open a can of fizzy drink?
options: Because the solubility of the gas increases
Because the gas is insoluble in water
Because the gas is dissolved under pressure hence it comes out when pressure is decreased
Because the solubility of the gas decreases at high pressure
rationales: Incorrect: decreasing pressure does not increase the gas's solubility in the drink.
Incorrect: the gas is dissolved in the drink before the can is opened.
Correct: opening the can lowers pressure, so dissolved gas escapes.
Incorrect: gas solubility increases, not decreases, when pressure is high.

quiz.stem:
Q6.7. The following reaction is performed in a closed vessel.

CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

How the equilibrium will be affected if you increase the pressure?
options: The forward reaction will be favoured
The backward reaction will be favoured
No effect on backward reaction
No effect on forward or backward reaction
rationales: Incorrect: the forward side has more gas molecules, so higher pressure does not favour it.
Correct: the backward direction reduces the amount of gas and is favoured by increased pressure.
Incorrect: increased pressure affects the equilibrium direction in this reaction.
Incorrect: pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, so it does have an effect.

quiz.stem: Q6.8. When a reaction will become a reversible one?
options: If the activation energy of the forward reaction is comparable to that of backward reaction
If the activation energy of the forward reaction is higher than that of backward reaction
If the activation energy of the forward reaction is lower than that of backward reaction
If the enthalpy change of both the reactions is zero.
rationales: Correct: comparable activation energies make the forward and backward processes possible under suitable conditions.
Incorrect: a higher forward activation energy alone is not the stated condition for reversibility.
Incorrect: a lower forward activation energy alone is not the stated condition for reversibility.
Incorrect: zero enthalpy change is not a requirement for a reaction to be reversible.

quiz.stem: Q6.10. What will happen to the concentrations of the products if a reversible reaction at equilibrium is not disturbed?
options: They will remain constant
They will keep on increasing
They will keep on decreasing
They will remain constant for some time and then start decreasing
rationales: Correct: at undisturbed equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal, so product concentrations remain constant.
Incorrect: products do not keep accumulating at equilibrium.
Incorrect: products are not continually consumed overall at equilibrium.
Incorrect: if the system remains undisturbed, the equilibrium concentrations remain constant.

rubric.how: State that heating favours the reactant side for ammonia formation.

rubric.description: Decreasing temperature drives ammonia equilibrium forward.
rubric.why: This correctly predicts the direction of the ammonia equilibrium after cooling.
rubric.how: State that cooling favours ammonia formation.

written.text: Synthesis of ammonia gas is very important industrially because it is used in the preparation of urea fertilizer. Explain the conditions you will use to get the maximum yield of ammonia.
modelAnswer: Use high pressure because 4 moles of reacting gases form 2 moles of product gas, so pressure favours the forward direction.
Use a lower temperature because formation of ammonia is exothermic in the forward direction.
Remove or liquefy ammonia as it forms to drive the reaction towards further ammonia production.
Use a catalyst to increase the rates of both reactions and reduce the time taken to reach equilibrium; it does not change the equilibrium yield.
written.followUp: What will happen if the gas mixture is compressed?

rubric.description: Use high pressure.
rubric.why: High pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles, which is the ammonia side.
rubric.how: Explain that the forward reaction makes fewer moles of gas, so high pressure favours ammonia.

rubric.description: Use lower temperature to favour the exothermic forward direction.
rubric.why: Cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction described in the section.
rubric.how: Link lower temperature to increased ammonia formation.

rubric.description: Withdraw or liquefy ammonia as it forms.
rubric.why: Removing product drives the reaction towards further product formation.
rubric.how: State that ammonia is removed or liquefied as it forms.

rubric.description: Use a catalyst to reduce the time to equilibrium.
rubric.why: A catalyst helps reach equilibrium sooner, which is useful in production.
rubric.how: State its rate or time benefit without claiming that it changes equilibrium yield.

rubric.description: A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or yield.
rubric.why: This correctly distinguishes a catalyst's effect on reaction time from its effect on yield.
rubric.how: Clarify that a catalyst speeds attainment but does not raise the equilibrium yield.

written.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
In static equilibrium, there is no ongoing reaction or movement.
written.followUp:

rubric.description: State that forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.why: This identifies what continues in dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.how: Mention both continuing reactions and equal rates.

rubric.description: State that static equilibrium has no ongoing reaction or movement.
rubric.why: This distinguishes static equilibrium from dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.how: Contrast dynamic activity with no ongoing change.

written.text:
How the following reversible reaction will be affected if its temperature is increased?

Electricity

2H₂O(l) ⇌ 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
modelAnswer: The forward decomposition of water is endothermic.
On increasing temperature, the forward reaction is favoured.
The amounts of H₂ and O₂ increase.

rubric.description: Explain that added heat favours the endothermic direction.
rubric.why: The direction favoured by added heat must be identified.
rubric.how: Name the forward direction and relate it to heat absorption.

rubric.description: State that more hydrogen and oxygen are formed.
rubric.why: The answer should state the effect on the products.
rubric.how: Identify both gaseous products.

written.text: How can you get the maximum yield in a reversible reaction?
modelAnswer: Select suitable temperature and pressure conditions to favour the forward reaction.
Increase the concentration of reactants or remove products as they form.
These changes shift the equilibrium towards the products and increase the yield.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: State that conditions should favour the forward reaction.
rubric.why: Maximum yield requires equilibrium to favour product formation.
rubric.how: Refer to shifting equilibrium towards the products.

rubric.description: Name suitable changes such as removing product or adjusting pressure, temperature, or concentration.
rubric.why: Give a practical way of adjusting the equilibrium position.
rubric.how: Give at least one relevant condition or product-removal method.

written.text: How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
modelAnswer: Add a catalyst to the reaction mixture.
The catalyst increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions.
The equilibrium position is reached sooner, but its position does not change.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: Name a catalyst.
rubric.why: A catalyst is the standard way to make equilibrium be reached sooner.
rubric.how: State that a catalyst is added.

rubric.description: Explain that both reaction rates increase and equilibrium is reached sooner.
rubric.why: The explanation must show that both directions are sped up without shifting equilibrium.
rubric.how: Mention both directions or both rates.

written.text:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)
modelAnswer: The reactant side has 2 moles of gas: 1 mole N₂ + 1 mole O₂.
The product side has 2 moles of gas: 2 moles NO.
Increasing pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: State that pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.
rubric.why: The equilibrium shift must be stated.
rubric.how: Clearly state that neither direction is favoured.

rubric.description: Compare the total gaseous moles on each side.
rubric.why: Equal gas amounts on both sides explain the result.
rubric.how: State that each side has two moles of gas.

written.text: Why are some reactions irreversible while others are reversible?
modelAnswer: A reaction is reversible when its products can react to form the original reactants under suitable conditions.
Some reactions are effectively irreversible because the reverse reaction is negligible, or because products escape or are very stable.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: Explain that products can react back to form reactants.
rubric.why: This describes the defining possibility in a reversible reaction.
rubric.how: Mention a backward reaction under suitable conditions.

rubric.description: Explain why some reactions proceed effectively only forward.
rubric.why: This distinguishes reactions whose reverse is negligible or hindered.
rubric.how: Mention negligible reverse reaction, escaping products, or stable products.

written.text: Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?
modelAnswer: Combustion forms stable products and releases energy.
These products do not readily react back to form the original fuel and oxygen, so combustion is generally irreversible.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: State that combustion forms stable products.
rubric.why: Stable products help explain why the reverse reaction is not readily observed.
rubric.how: Use the idea of stable products.

rubric.description: State that products do not readily reform fuel and oxygen.
rubric.why: This explains why combustion generally does not reverse under ordinary conditions.
rubric.how: Describe the reverse reaction as not readily occurring.

written.text: How do you know if a reaction is reversible or irreversible?
modelAnswer: A reversible reaction proceeds in both forward and backward directions, so products can reform reactants.
An irreversible reaction proceeds effectively in one direction under the stated conditions.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: Describe a reversible reaction as proceeding in both directions.
rubric.why: The possibility of a backward reaction identifies reversibility.
rubric.how: Mention products reforming reactants.

rubric.description: Describe an irreversible reaction as proceeding effectively in one direction.
rubric.why: This provides the contrast needed to identify an irreversible reaction.
rubric.how: State that a significant backward reaction does not occur.

written.text: Do the phase changes in water (solid to liquid, liquid to vapour) reversible or irreversible?
modelAnswer: The phase changes in water are reversible.
Ice melts to liquid water, and liquid water freezes to ice.
Liquid water evaporates to vapour, and vapour condenses to liquid water.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: State that the phase changes are reversible.
rubric.why: The answer must classify the phase changes.
rubric.how: Use the word reversible.

rubric.description: Give at least one pair of opposite changes.
rubric.why: Reverse phase changes support the classification.
rubric.how: Name melting/freezing or evaporation/condensation.

written.text:
How can you drive the reversible reaction at equilibrium?

(a) in the forward direction  
(b) in the backward direction
modelAnswer: (a) Increase the concentration of a reactant or remove a product to drive the reaction forward.
(b) Increase the concentration of a product or remove a reactant to drive the reaction backward.
Pressure and temperature can also be changed when they favour the required direction.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: Give a condition that favours the forward direction.
rubric.why: The forward change must shift equilibrium towards products.
rubric.how: For example, increase reactant concentration or remove product.

rubric.description: Give a condition that favours the backward direction.
rubric.why: The backward change must shift equilibrium towards reactants.
rubric.how: For example, increase product concentration or remove reactant.

written.text: Explain how the rates of forward and backward reactions change when the system approaches equilibrium.
modelAnswer: As reactants are used up, the rate of the forward reaction decreases.
As products form, the rate of the backward reaction increases.
At equilibrium, the two rates become equal and the concentrations remain constant.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: State that the forward rate decreases as reactants are used.
rubric.why: The change in forward rate must be described.
rubric.how: Describe the forward reaction as slowing.

rubric.description: State that the backward rate increases until it equals the forward rate.
rubric.why: The increasing reverse rate and equality at equilibrium complete the explanation.
rubric.how: Mention both increasing backward rate and equal rates at equilibrium.

written.text: Describe the effect of a catalyst on the reversible reaction.
modelAnswer: A catalyst increases the rates of both the forward and backward reactions.
The system reaches equilibrium sooner.
The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or the equilibrium yield.
written.followUp:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)

rubric.description: State that it increases both reaction rates.
rubric.why: A catalyst acts on both directions of a reversible reaction.
rubric.how: Mention both forward and backward reactions.

rubric.description: State that equilibrium is reached sooner but its position does not change.
rubric.why: The answer must distinguish reaction speed from equilibrium position.
rubric.how: Include both effects.

written.text: Study the effect of heat on hydrated copper sulphate. Why does this salt look coloured and why does it lose colour upon heating?
modelAnswer: Hydrated copper sulphate is blue because it contains water of crystallisation.
On heating, it loses water and forms anhydrous copper sulphate.
Anhydrous copper sulphate is white, so the salt loses its blue colour.
Adding water to the anhydrous salt restores the blue colour.

rubric.why: This explains the original colour of hydrated copper sulphate.
rubric.how: State the colour and the role of hydration.

rubric.description: Explain what heating does to the hydrated salt.
rubric.why: Heating removes the water responsible for hydration.
rubric.how: Say that it loses water of crystallisation.

rubric.description: Name the white anhydrous product.
rubric.why: The product and its observed colour must be identified.
rubric.how: State that anhydrous copper sulphate is white.

rubric.description: State that adding water restores the blue colour.
rubric.why: Rehydration demonstrates the reversible colour change.
rubric.how: Describe the colour returning after water is added.

written.text: Synthesis of ammonia gas is very important industrially because it is used in the preparation of urea fertilizer. Explain the conditions you will use to get the maximum yield of ammonia.
modelAnswer: The reaction is N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
Use nitrogen and hydrogen in a 1:3 ratio.
Use high pressure because the product side has fewer gas molecules.
Use a moderate temperature of about 450°C and an iron catalyst.
Remove ammonia as it forms to shift the equilibrium towards further product formation.

rubric.why: Correct reactant proportions support ammonia synthesis.
rubric.how: State one part nitrogen to three parts hydrogen.

rubric.description: State that high pressure favours ammonia formation.
rubric.why: High pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.
rubric.how: Link increased pressure to the product side.

rubric.description: Give the moderate operating temperature, about 450°C.
rubric.why: The moderate temperature gives a practical balance of yield and reaction rate.
rubric.how: State about 450°C or identify a moderate temperature.

rubric.description: Name the iron catalyst.
rubric.why: The catalyst helps the process reach equilibrium faster.
rubric.how: State that iron is used as a catalyst.

rubric.description: State that ammonia is removed as it forms.
rubric.why: Removing product shifts equilibrium towards further ammonia formation.
rubric.how: Explain that removing product promotes the forward reaction.
